titulo: ETFs in Brazil in 2025: Real Growth, Still Indeterminable Causes
resumo: In December 2025, 919,000 individual investors held ETF positions in Brazil — almost double the figure from two years earlier. The asset class's assets went from R$54 billion to more than R$91 billion over the…
corpo:
In December 2025, 919,000 individual investors held ETF positions in Brazil — almost double the figure from two years earlier. The asset class's total assets went from R$54 billion to more than R$91 billion over the year. Fixed income ETFs, which until 2024 occupied a marginal share of the sector, became the center of gravity for inflows.

There are two explanations with a real mechanism behind this growth. The problem is that both occurred within the same 12-to-18-month window — and public data does not separate the weight of each.

This article does not pick a winner. It explains why doing so is not possible with the available data, and describes what would be needed to resolve the question.

What Grew, When, and Who Bought

The jump in assets mixes two things that need to be separated: new money and mark-to-market appreciation. In a year of high Selic rates, part of the increase is appreciation of assets already in the portfolio, not inflow. That is why the gross figure is not the most important metric. The relevant metric is the change in investor composition — and that change is unambiguous.

In January 2025, individual and institutional investors split ETF holdings in close-to-even proportions — about R$19 billion for individuals versus R$34 billion for institutions, in total assets of R$58 billion. Over the course of the year, individual investor holdings grew 49%. By December, individuals accounted for between 78% and 81% of the ETF industry's total assets. Fixed income ETFs specifically closed the year with 721,700 investors and R$26.9 billion in custody — a figure with no public breakdown by investor type.

The year closed with net inflows of R$13 billion, according to B3's Annual ETF Report — a reversal of two straight years of net redemptions. That figure is net inflow: subscriptions minus redemptions, excluding market appreciation. The R$37 billion in total asset growth (from R$54B to R$91B) combines that net flow with the appreciation of assets in the portfolio. The change in composition that accompanies this flow is verifiable and is not explained by mark-to-market: institutional investors did not disappear from the portfolio; they were diluted by retail growth.

The product shelf also expanded: 62 new ETFs were listed on B3 over the course of the year — versus 16 in 2024 and 13 in 2023 — broadening access to strategies previously restricted to large allocators.

This rules out the reading that the driver was institutional. Retail was the vector of the compositional change. But it does not say — yet — why.

Four Explanations, Two Ruled Out

There are four candidate explanations. Two fail the timing test. Two survive.

One candidate explanation is supply: more products, simpler platforms, lower minimum tickets. It fails because the first fixed income ETF listed in Brazil, IMAB11, has existed since May 2019. Supply was available for five years without meaningful traction. If supply were the cause, growth would have started in 2019. It is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one.

Another candidate is "investor maturation" — a recurring claim in market reports. It fails because it has neither a mechanism nor a date: it describes the result and labels it a cause. "The investor became more mature" explains ETF growth the same way "the teams scored more goals" explains a final score. It is true and it is useless.

Two remain.

Distribution friction. The dominant channel in the Brazilian market is the investment advisor (assessor de investimentos), compensated through commissions and rebates on the products they distribute. ETFs pay low or zero rebates. Where this compensation logic prevails, there is a structural incentive not to offer ETFs to the client — not out of bad faith, but by design of the model. The market today operates under three basic configurations: the commission-paid advisor, still predominant; the advisor operating under a fee-based model tied to a financial institution; and the securities consultant (consultor de valores mobiliários) registered with CVM, who works for a fixed fee and can serve clients at any institution. CVM Resolutions 178 and 179, in effect between November 2024 and January 2025, imposed transparency on compensation and demarcated these models more precisely. Over the same period, the base of consultants registered with CVM grew 28%. The decline in friction, in this reading, comes from the advance of fee-based models in their various forms — the institutionally tied advisor who began charging for the service, or the independent consultant — and from the migration to the self-sufficient investor, who dispenses with any intermediary.

Product merit under high interest rates. Fixed income ETFs deliver a measurable tax advantage over traditional fixed income: no come-cotas, no IOF, with exchange liquidity and low cost. In traditional funds, the tax authority withholds tax twice a year, reducing the capital working for the investor. In an ETF, tax is only due upon sale. The compounded advantage, calculated under the regime in effect after MP 1,303 lapsed in October 2025, reaches 0.92 percentage points over two years, 2.8 points over five, and 6.2 points over ten. With the Selic at an elevated level in 2024 and 2025, this advantage applied on top of a high nominal return, making it even more legible in the investor's net account.

The Problem That Prevents Picking a Winner

Here is the knot. The Selic rose and the channel changed in the same window: 2024 to 2025. In statistics, this has a name — collinearity. In market practice, the problem is simpler to state: when two forces push the same car at the same time, you cannot look at the speed and pin down which of the two pushed harder.

Consider the investor who put money into a Tesouro Selic ETF at the end of 2025. Did they do it because high interest rates made the tax exemption irresistible on paper? Or did they do it because, for the first time, they reached a channel — a fee-based consultant, or simply the home broker — that had no financial incentive to hide that product from them?

The question has no answer in open data. With the Selic high and the channel shift occurring at the same time, any observed ETF growth is compatible with product merit, with the decline in commercial friction, or with both in a proportion that public series simply do not isolate. Claiming that "it was the channel shift" or "it was the tax merit" based on these series is not analysis — it is narrative choice dressed up as conclusion.

Declaring this indeterminacy is not weakness. Exposing that the market is buying a manufactured certainty is the real advantage of the analysis.

What the International Evidence Says — and Does Not Say

The literature on the effect of the distribution model on asset allocation is consistent in direction.

Christoffersen, Evans, and Musto (2013), in the Journal of Finance, showed with data from U.S. funds between 1993 and 2009 that payments to brokers are associated with greater inflows into funds with worse future performance. The conflict of interest in the commission-based model produces adverse selection for the investor.

When the United Kingdom banned commissions to advisors in 2013 (Retail Distribution Review), Morningstar analysts directly linked the ban to the migration toward passive funds. The Netherlands achieved a similar result: a decline in product costs beyond the eliminated commission, with a shift toward passive management above the average of other European countries.

Sebastian, Noth, and Grafe (University of Regensburg, 2023), in a panel of 38 OECD countries between 1997 and 2020, estimated a difference in wealth returns of 1.5% to 2% per year between countries with and without a commission ban — with an estimated cumulative loss for Europe of €375 billion per year. The study drew strong criticism from the financial industry, which should be noted by anyone citing it.

The limit of the analogy is precise: the United Kingdom and the Netherlands imposed the ban through state coercion, forcing immediate migration. Brazil operates in a free market, with competition between the commission-based and fee-based models. CVM Resolutions 178 and 179 did not ban commissions — they imposed transparency. The international literature proves that the direction of the effect exists. It does not prove that the Brazilian transition will have the speed of the ban cases, nor that it is inevitable.

What the Self-Sufficient Investor Changes in the Equation

There is a point that the channel narrative does not directly resolve.

The individual who bought an ETF in 2025 could have arrived through three paths: a fee-based consultant, a commission-paid advisor (structurally improbable, but not impossible), or a self-sufficient investor — opening the home broker, reading about come-cotas, buying alone, with no intermediary at all.

There is no public cross-reference between ETF inflows and the originating channel. B3 and ANBIMA publish ETF growth. CVM publishes consultant growth. No one cross-references the two databases.

If the flow is predominantly self-sufficient, the narrative of the "fee-based revolution" loses the prominence attributed to it. The product simply sold itself on its own merit, without needing a new type of advisor to reach the investor. This does not mean channel friction is irrelevant — the investor who chose the home broker also dispensed with the commission-paid advisor, which is itself a form of reduced friction. But it dissolves the specific claim that fee-based consultants were the central vector of growth.

In this reading, the channel explanation and the product-merit explanation not only converge: they become nearly indistinguishable. A good product in a frictionless channel is, at the same time, a product that won on merit and a channel that stopped blocking it. Calling them separate causes becomes a distinction without available empirical support.

What Would Settle the Question

Waiting for the Selic to fall does not solve the problem. A drop in interest rates does not switch off the product's merit — it merely trades the appeal of a high nominal return for the appeal of relatively low cost, since an active fund's fee weighs more heavily when the CDI shrinks. An ETF withstanding a rate cut is compatible with product merit the entire time. The time-based test is inconclusive by construction.

The valid isolation is by comparing groups, not by time. At a given moment, with the same Selic, the same tax regime, and the same products available, ETF merit is identical for all investors. If merit is the driver, adoption should be similar between clients of commission-paid advisors and clients of fee-based consultants. If channel friction is the driver, adoption diverges: high in the rebate-free channel, low in the commission-paid one.

Two data sets would make this test possible. The first: ETF adoption by distribution channel, controlled for investor profile — this would isolate the effect of the conflict of interest between professionals. The second: a breakdown of ETF purchase flow by order origin, advised account versus self-directed account, within the same platforms — this would measure how much of the phenomenon goes through any intermediary at all.

Neither data set is available in public sources. The market today tracks the phenomenon through aggregated databases, without cross-referencing flow origin by channel. Until these databases converge publicly, attributing ETF growth to a single cause — whether the advisory model or the tax merit — will remain in the realm of speculation.

What the available metrics allow us to state without ambiguity is that the structural shift in allocation is real. The jump to 919,000 investors and the R$13 billion in net inflows prove that retail has definitively adopted the vehicle. Whether through the legibility of the tax gain, the natural decline in commercial friction, or — what is mathematically more likely — the indivisible combination of both forces in the same time window, the ETF has stopped being a secondary-shelf product and become the portfolio's center of gravity.

The author is not a credentialed securities analyst. The analyses presented here are retrospective, based on public data, and should not be used as a basis for investment decisions.
